As part of my MasterClass Executive certification, I recently completed the chapter "The Coaching Mindset for Leaders" within the Leadership Principles course. The chapter brought together three distinct perspectives on leadership, coaching, and behavioral science.

Course Instructors
Maureen Chiquet — Former Global CEO of Chanel and board director at global consumer brands
Michael Bungay Stanier — Founder of Box of Crayons and author of The Coaching Habit
Ayelet Fishbach — UChicago Booth professor, author of Get It Done, and expert on human motivation and behavior

What made this especially interesting to me was the combination of executive leadership, coaching, and behavioral science. One realization stayed with me throughout the chapter: many situations we experience in leadership are not isolated personal experiences. They are patterns.

A struggling employee, an unmotivated volunteer, a student constantly seeking answers, a high performer losing energy, or a leader who feels responsible for solving every problem can seem like a completely individual situation. Yet when we study leadership more systematically, we begin to recognize that similar challenges appear across classrooms, companies, nonprofit organizations, and teams around the world.

This raises an important question: if these patterns exist across organizations, how can education and technology help us recognize them, learn from them, and respond more effectively?

From Solving Problems to Developing People

One of the central ideas of the coaching mindset is that a leader's responsibility is not always to provide the answer. Sometimes leadership means helping another person develop the ability to discover the answer themselves.

The chapter describes this as drawing out someone's capability rather than substituting our own. This made me reflect on my own leadership style. Of the leadership tendencies discussed, I recognize myself most strongly in the SAVE IT mindset. When I see someone struggling, my instinct is often to intervene quickly, remove the obstacle, provide the solution, and prevent the person from struggling longer than necessary.

The intention is positive. But leadership requires another question: is solving someone's problem immediately always the best way to help them grow?

My experience in education gradually changed the way I approach this. As a teacher and Student Council Coordinator, and through years of nonprofit leadership and Learning and Development work, I have increasingly tried to transform my educational philosophy into a leadership philosophy: help people discover rather than simply provide.

If the leader constantly becomes the answer, people can become dependent on the leader. If the leader develops people's ability to think, evaluate, and decide, the organization gradually develops more leaders.

Coaching Is Structured Leadership

Asking questions does not mean that leaders should stop sharing their knowledge. The chapter's GROW framework provides a structure for helping people think before the leader jumps directly to advice.

GROW Framework
Goal What are we trying to achieve?
Reality What is actually happening right now?
Options What different paths are available?
Will What will you do next, and when?

What interests me most is the sequence. Expertise remains important, but it does not always need to come first. Sometimes the most valuable contribution a leader can make is asking the question that causes another person to think differently.

I see this in education almost every day. Teaching cannot simply be about transferring correct answers from the teacher to the student. Education should develop the ability to question, analyze, experiment, make decisions, reflect, and eventually operate independently. I increasingly believe that leadership should follow the same principle.

Understanding People Before Managing Performance

Another concept that resonated with me was the Zone of Genius, where someone's capabilities intersect with work that gives them energy. The chapter connects this idea with three important intrinsic motivators:

  • Autonomy: having meaningful ownership over how work is done
  • Mastery: becoming better at work that matters
  • Purpose: understanding how the work contributes to something larger

This is particularly relevant when assigning responsibilities. Two people can be equally committed while contributing in completely different ways. One person may naturally organize people and systems. Another may communicate exceptionally well. Someone else may identify problems early. Another may become energized when developing new ideas.

Leadership becomes stronger when we stop asking only "What is this person good at?" and begin asking: "Where can this person contribute, grow, and remain energized?"

Feedback Should Create Movement

The chapter's discussion of Radical Candor emphasizes the need to combine care with challenge. The SBI model (Situation, Behavior, Impact) encourages leaders to focus on observable actions and their consequences rather than making judgments about someone's personality.

For me, successful feedback should help answer questions such as: Did the person understand what I meant? Do they understand the impact of the behavior? Do they know what should change next? Did the conversation create clarity? Did I preserve enough trust for future conversations?

Feedback is not successful simply because the leader delivered it. What matters is what the other person understood and what happens afterward.

Behavior Is Information

The chapter's discussion of burnout reinforced this idea further. Burnout is presented through patterns involving exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced efficacy. Rather than assuming someone simply needs rest, leaders are encouraged to examine what may be happening within the work environment and have structured conversations about possible causes and changes.

  • Withdrawal is information
  • Motivation is information
  • Frustration is information
  • Repeated mistakes are information
  • Energy is information
  • Silence can also be information

Our responsibility as leaders is not to diagnose every behavior. But we should become better at observing patterns before reaching conclusions. This is where education becomes essential. Leadership development gives us frameworks that allow us to recognize experiences that previously felt completely personal.

Where Technology Enters the Conversation

Technology is often presented primarily as a way to make organizations faster. Today we use it to automate tasks, summarize information, generate content, analyze data, organize knowledge, and save time. All of these benefits matter. But I believe the larger opportunity is different.

Technology can help us recognize patterns that individuals and organizations often experience in isolation. Imagine learning and leadership environments where technology helps identify recurring patterns in engagement, motivation, feedback, professional development, team dynamics, and leadership challenges.

Technology should not make leadership less human. It should help us understand humans better.

Human judgment should remain at the center. The purpose should not be to allow technology to make every leadership decision for us. Its greater value may be helping us see what we would otherwise miss. One teacher's experience could contribute to another teacher's learning. One organization's challenge could become useful knowledge for another organization. Patterns that normally remain isolated could become opportunities for collective learning.

The Intersection I Want to Explore

My own journey has gradually brought together education, Learning and Development, leadership training, artificial intelligence, and EdTech. My background also includes leadership and collaboration training, AI evaluation and rubric design, organizational change, teaching, volunteer development, and Learning and Development work.

I increasingly see these not as separate professional interests, but as different parts of one larger question: how can learning design, leadership, and EdTech work together to develop human capability?

Beyond Answers

As artificial intelligence continues to make information more accessible, having the answer may become less important as a leadership advantage. Other capabilities may become increasingly important: asking better questions, recognizing potential, understanding motivation, developing judgment, identifying patterns, coaching people through uncertainty, and creating environments where people can grow.

"How can I solve this for you?"
→
"How can I help you develop the ability to solve it?"

That shift matters to executives, teachers, Learning and Development professionals, nonprofit leaders, mentors, and anyone responsible for developing people. It also represents the direction I want to continue pursuing professionally, at the intersection of education, leadership, Learning and Development, artificial intelligence, and EdTech.

The future of technology should not be about replacing the leader inside people. It should help us discover and develop it.
